samasa.vigraha: स्वस्य चित्तं स्वचित्तम्; स्वचित्ते आयत्तः स्वचित्तायत्तः; तस्य भावः स्वचित्तायत्तता, ताम्
samasa.type: saptamī tatpuruṣa (स्वचित्तायत्त) containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (स्वचित्त), made abstract with -ता
samasa.literal: the state of being dependent on one’s own mind
samasa.sense: self-control; विना ‘without’ it means ‘beyond my control, against my will’

samasa.literal: of one whose kingdom has gone
in the limbs of the kingdom
samasa.sense: every part of the realm he once ruled

morph.note: A noun built on an inflected form: the genitive मम ‘of me, mine’ + the abstract suffix -त्व. ‘Mine-ness’: the feeling that something belongs to me. The same idea returns as ममता in 1.53.
Dative of result: ‘for the grief of (my) mind’, i.e. so that it pains me.
Abstract noun in -ता on a compound: the whole phrase ‘dependent on one’s own mind’ is turned into a state, then governed by विना.

mantras.anvaya: यत् गतराज्यस्य मे अखिलेषु अपि राज्याङ्गेषु ममत्वं (अस्ति), (मम) मनसः दुःखाय, स्वचित्तायत्ततां विना, …
mantras.anvaya_en: A यत् clause (‘that …’), nominal, with ‘is’ understood; its subject is ममत्वम्. It is taken up by किम् एतत् in 1.42.
mantras.lit: That — to the grief of my mind, without (its) being under the control of my own mind — there is in me, whose kingdom is gone, a sense of ‘mine’ even toward all the limbs of the kingdom,
mantras.tr: My kingdom is gone, yet I still feel that every part of it is mine — against my own will, and to my mind’s distress,
mantras.tr_note: The Sanskrit is a ‘that …’ clause completed by ‘what is this?’ in 1.42; the translation makes it a statement. ‘Against my own will’ renders स्वचित्तायत्ततां विना.

comm.t: Now the king speaks of himself. He asked the merchant why he still loved those who had wronged him (1.27–28); here he admits the same bondage: he has lost his kingdom and cannot stop feeling it is his.

‘Limbs of the kingdom’ is a term of Indian political thought, where a state has seven limbs: the king, ministers, territory, fort, treasury, army and ally. The king’s earlier worries (1.12–14) touch several of them: his city, his servants, his elephant, his treasury.

ā + a → ā. Read as two words: ‘as of one who does not know’.
Final t before m becomes n.
-aiḥ is sounded -air before the voiced d and bh, and becomes -ais before t; तथा + उज्झितः gives तथोज्झितः.

samasa.sense: an ignorant man; ज्ञ ‘knowing’ is itself a kṛt noun from √ज्ञा
a respectful address to Medhas (compare पार्थिवसत्तमः, 1.37)

morph.note: Genitive of the present participle जानत्, agreeing with मे in 1.41: ‘of me, though knowing’. It echoes the merchant’s जानन्नपि (1.32).
दार ‘wife’ is masculine and used only in the plural; one wife is meant.
Past participle of नि + √कृ ‘to bring down, to wrong’; with उज्झितः the two participles describe the merchant, the verb ‘is’ understood.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) मुनिसत्तम, जानतः अपि (मे) अज्ञस्य यथा (ममत्वम्) — एतत् किम्? अयं च पुत्रैः दारैः भृत्यैः निकृतः तथा उज्झितः, …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the king’s own case (‘though knowing, as if not knowing’) and asks ‘what is this?’. The second opens the merchant’s case, continued in 1.43.
mantras.lit: — (in me,) though knowing, as in one who does not know: what is this, O best of sages? And this man has been wronged by sons, wife and servants, and likewise abandoned,
mantras.tr: though I know better, as if I did not. What is this, best of sages? And this man too has been wronged and cast off by his sons, his wife and his servants,

comm.t: The king states his own paradox in the words of the merchant: knowing, yet behaving like one who does not know (compare जानन्नपि, 1.32). Then he presents the merchant’s case beside his own.

sandhi.type: visarga sandhi (special rule for एषः); vowel sandhi
sandhi.rule: एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि (6.1.132); अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः (6.1.101)
sandhi.note: The visarga of एषः is dropped before the consonant t; तथा + अहम् → तथाहम्.
au before a becomes āv (द्वावपि); i before a becomes y (अप्यत्यन्त-).

samasa.alt: अत्यन्त is itself a prādi compound, अन्तम् अतिक्रान्तम् ‘going beyond the end’, used as an adverb.

morph.note: Masculine nominative of हार्दिन् (in-stem: the n drops and the i lengthens), the word used in the neuter (हार्दि) in 1.32 of the merchant’s mind.
Normally a prefix (अति-), here a free adverb ‘exceedingly’, a usage found in epic and Purāṇic verse; it goes with हार्दी.
दुःखित ‘pained’ is दुःख + the taddhita -इत (‘in whom grief has arisen’), dual to match द्वौ.

mantras.anvaya: (अयं) स्वजनेन च संत्यक्तः, तथा अपि तेषु अति हार्दी। एवम् एषः तथा अहं च द्वौ अपि अत्यन्तदुःखितौ, …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line finishes the merchant’s case: participle संत्यक्तः, then a concessive clause with हार्दी. The second sums up both men; the nominal predicate अत्यन्तदुःखितौ continues into 1.44.
mantras.lit: and deserted by his kin; even so he is exceedingly affectionate toward them. Thus this man and likewise I — both of us are deeply afflicted,
mantras.tr: and deserted by his kin; yet he loves them dearly. So he and I alike are both in deep distress,

comm.t: The king sets the two cases side by side and draws the sum: both men are in great pain, and for the same reason. The next verse names it.

flags.uncertain: तथाप्यति is split तथा अपि अति, with अति as a free adverb qualifying हार्दी. This is a point of interpretation, not of reading: the uncommon free adverb अति could also be taken loosely with the whole clause (‘even so, too much’); either way he loves them excessively.

samasa.literal: in which the fault has been seen
samasa.sense: a thing whose flaw is already plain

samasa.vigraha: ममत्वेन आकृष्टं ममत्वाकृष्टम्; ममत्वाकृष्टं मानसं ययोः तौ
samasa.literal: the two whose minds are drawn by mine-ness
samasa.sense: pulled by possessiveness against their judgement

morph.note: Genitive dual of ज्ञानिन् ‘one who has knowledge’ (the same form serves as locative dual). ‘Of us two who know’: the king includes himself and the merchant.
आकृष्ट is the past participle of आ + √कृष् ‘to drag’. Compare 1.12, where the king alone was ममत्वाकृष्टचेतनः; now both men are.

mantras.anvaya: (आवां) दृष्टदोषे अपि विषये ममत्वाकृष्टमानसौ (स्वः)। तत्, महाभाग, एतत् किम्, यत् ज्ञानिनोः अपि (आवयोः) मोहः (भवति)?
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the description of the two (from 1.43); the second asks the question proper, with a यत् clause explaining एतत्.
mantras.lit: — our minds dragged by possessiveness toward an object even though its fault has been seen. So what is this, O blessed one, that there is delusion even in (us) two who know?
mantras.tr: our minds dragged by the sense of ‘mine’ toward things whose faults we have plainly seen. Then what is this, blessed one — that even we, who know, are deluded?

comm.t: The question of the first carita, in its full form: why does delusion (मोह) persist in those who know? The king and the merchant both see the fault in what they cling to, and cling still.
The sage’s answer turns on two words of this verse. He takes up विषय at once (1.47–48), and he names the source of the मोह of ‘even those who know’ as Mahāmāyā (1.55, ज्ञानिनामपि चेतांसि).

samasa.sense: unable to judge rightly, though not unknowing

morph.note: Singular, agreeing with the nearer genitive अस्य, but the sense applies to both speakers: ‘of me and of him, (each) blind in discernment’.
Abstract noun in -ता from मूढ, the past participle of √मुह् ‘to be bewildered’ — the same root as मोह (1.44).

mantras.anvaya: मम अस्य च विवेकान्धस्य एषा मूढता भवति।
mantras.anvaya_en: A simple sentence completing the question of 1.44: subject मूढता with एषा, possessors मम अस्य च, verb भवति.
mantras.lit: — this bewilderment comes to me and to him, blind in discernment.
mantras.tr: — this bewilderment, in him and in me, blind as we are to discernment.
mantras.tr_note: ‘as we are’ renders the singular विवेकान्धस्य applied to both.

comm.t: The king’s question ends. He distinguishes two things: they have knowledge (ज्ञान, 1.44) but lack discernment (विवेक), and so they are bewildered. The sage begins his answer in 1.47.

A modern reading: the king’s diagnosis is precise. Information is not the problem; the faculty that weighs it and lets go is. The rest of the chapter traces that failure to a power larger than the two men.
